fif

Game StrategyArithmeticLogic
Game: You and the computer take turns picking numbers from 1 to 9; whoever first holds three numbers that add up to 15 wins.
How to play: Press a number to take it. The computer answers at once. Tick Computer moves first and press Start if you want it to begin.

Look for the math

Fif looks like a game about adding, but it is TicTacToe in disguise.

The magic square

There are exactly eight ways to write 15 as a sum of three different numbers from 1 to 9: 1+5+9, 1+6+8, 2+4+9, 2+5+8, 2+6+7, 3+4+8, 3+5+7, 4+5+6. The logic test found them by trying all 84 triples. Write the nine numbers in the magic square 4 9 2 / 3 5 7 / 8 1 6 and these eight triples are exactly its three rows, three columns and two diagonals. Tick Show the magic square and the game looks like TicTacToe, with the 5 in the centre.

Perfect play is a draw

The test solved the whole game tree: with perfect play the game is a draw, as in TicTacToe. The computer is not perfect. It only looks one move ahead, taking a win if it has one and avoiding a move that lets you win at once, so you can beat it: against it with its errors switched off, the test found 16 winning sequences of your moves when you move first and 6 when it does, and many more that lose, as you would expect. You win by making a fork, two threats at once.

The computer errs

The page says the computer errs with probability 1/20. In the applet, each free square it looks at has a 1 in 20 chance of being taken straight away without a check. So a missed block is more likely than 1 in 20: in the test the computer blocks a threat only about 82% of the time in a typical position, and takes a win about 90% of the time (0.95²). The test computed those exactly.

The applet's box is called I move first, and the page explains that checking it makes the computer start; it is called Computer moves first here. Scores are kept until you leave the page, and Clear does not reset them. After a finished game, pressing a number starts a new one with that move.

Take 5 first. Then try to win by taking 4, and then 6 or 2, so that two lines are threatened at once.

Puzzle by Alexander Bogomolny (cut-the-knot.org)
